In the universe of Tolkien's works there was Iluvatar, the highest of the high, the equal to God, like the primordial Uranus in Greek mythos, he spawned the rest of the gods.

From his mind he created lesser reflections of aspects of himself. These were the Ainur, which were split into greater and lesser gods of the world. Like the Titans and the Gods of Greece, there is a difference in how powerful they are one on one. The greater gods were called Valar and the lesser Maiar.

Being a miniature reflection of just a fraction of Iluvatar, each of the Ainur thought and acted differently. They were made up of a different sliver of the highest power in existence, so the part that most loved to learn and make would be reflected in Aulë or Melkor, while the part loving to encourage growth and green things would be reflected within Yavanna.

When people talk about the fight between the Balrog and Gandalf they usually don't realize Gandalf is one of the Maiar, but even among those who do, a lot do not realize that as one of the Wizards, Gandalf was just a man.

Have I confused you yet?

The Balrog was one of the Maiar who followed the first Dark Lord, the rogue Valar called Morgoth. In order to better make use of their power they took on a form as fearsome and dangerous as they could. Pure fire and shadow with swords and whips, beautiful and terrible. All the Ainur could change form freely to suit their whims, and even breed with people and animals when they took the proper form. Except those that followed Morgoth - those eventually lost the ability to change form. The loss of the form changing is a direct result of what you could call their corruption. One's fall from grace removes the ability to freely change form.

Gandalf the Grey, Mithrandir, Stormcrow, the White.... Etc., was a being of the Maiar who under the instructions of the Valar went to Middle Earth to try and help undermine and overthrow the growing power of Sauron, without being obvious. This was because the last time the efforts of the Valar and Maiar were directly applied to the world, a fucking continent was ruined. Fearing the effects of such a conflict, they went lower key. They sent the five Istari, the wizards. There were four goals between the five - knowledge, compassion, animals, and undoing the effects of Sauron. The wizards in question were Saruman, Gandalf, Radagast, Morinehtar and Romestamo. The last two are largely unknown because their mission lead them into the lands controlled by Sauron. Each of the Istari's goals led them in different directions because they were Maiar of different aspects of Illuvatar's mind.

So, yes, we all agree at this point that both the Balrog and Gandalf are similar beings. But both being Maiar does not make them the same. One followed Melkor, the other did not. One is a pure manifestation of it's power, one is a limited and controlled form which allows for a proper disguise to let the wanderer walk amongst the peoples of Middle Earth freely.

The Istari were not pure representations of their power, they were instead disguised as old Human men. This is like taking on a handicap in golf, you don't sit on a level playing field.

When the Valar, as I said, fearing what would happen if they struck against Sauron, sent the Istari to try to fix the situation, it was meant to be a stealth operation.

Aulë, sorta the god of the Dwarves, their creator, and the master of making and crafting and a great fan of hidden secrets and knowledge, he sent Curumo, a Maia of his. In essense, a mini-mirror of his interests and skills. Independent of thought, self aware, but by nature he was one of Aule's spirits - the best of his in fact. He was Saruman, and as the most powerful of those being sent, as well as the most knowledgeable, he was appointed their leader.

Orome, the god of the hunt - he sent Alatar, as you know him, Morinehtar. He was sent because of all the Valar, Orome had the best knowledge of the East, where Sauron held the most sway. As a spirit of Orome's host, Alatar was also well verse in the region.

Olorin, or Gandalf the Grey, was requested by Manwe, the King of the Gods, pretty much Odin, which is kinda funny, since the character of Gandalf is in turn based on Odin and Olorin was one of Manwe's Maiar. Olorin did not want to go, he was weak and afraid of Sauron. Manwe selected Olorin because of all the Maiar, he was one of the few who really cared about the suffering of the people of Middle Earth, he was gentle and wise. He would spend time with Lorien and Nienna, the gods of visions and suffering, Nienna did not cause suffering, she would weep for every sad event that mortals were doomed to suffer. Because of this Gandalf was well versed in the pains of the mortals, while the others were more aloof. Nienna is the goddess of hope, because while one may suffer now, their is hope for a better future. She taught Olorin of this, and helped to form his essense. Lorien was able to teach him of how to inspire events, to conjure visions of a future. This is why Gandalf was so good at getting people to act.

Pallando, or to mortals Romestamo, was selected, not by Valar, but by Alatar, because they were close friends of the host of Orome.

Aiwendil was Yavanna's selection to round out the bunch, Yavanna is the goddess of animals and plants. Pretty much mother nature herself. He became known as Radagast.

All five were given human bodies, and all their power and knowledge were reduced greatly in these forms, so that they could not destroy the continent as the Valar had earlier done.

When they arrived at Middle Earth, Gandalf was recognised by Cirdan, an Elf lord, and he gave Gandalf a tool of great power, one of the three Elven Rings of Power - Nanya. It had the power to enkindle courage, and bring comfort and respite to peoples. Great for in wars, not so much in duels.

The great sword Glamdring that Gandalf gets in the Hobbit from the Troll's loot is ancient Elven, and extremely powerful. It was explicitly made to kill Orcs and to react to the taint of Melkor. The taint which made the Balrog of Moria permanently stuck in that form.

One of the proofs of this restrained nature of the Wizards is in Sharkey, when Saruman loses his position within the Wizards to Gandalf he does not have the ability to immediately return to the West or even change form. He is stuck an old man until his body is killed.

So, while they were both of the same core nature, these two were far from the same.

Gandalf was actually an old man who was really smart, kind and caring with a badass sword and a Ring of Power.

The Balrog was a lesser God gone mad.

So for many fans of The Lord of the Rings Gandalf seems like a very impressive man for killing a demon, for the more learned fans he is less impressive because he was afterall a god fighting another god... But for the fans who really dug into the lore, Gandalf is actually pretty impressive for an old man killing a god.

For those curious where all that lore comes from, the Appendixes of The Lord of the Rings and The Silmarillion itself are excellent places to find titbits of information.
